title: Is it legal to use OpenAI output to compile a smaller model?
question_text:
Is it legal to use OpenAI output to compile a smaller model?

The compilation step is very neat and I love the DSP paradym and was planning to implement it internally. But we not sure about a legal consideration. According to openai's terms of service
is not allowed.
Does this mean if I compile a model based on the outputs from GPT-4 to fine-tune a smaller opensource model that is used internally or used to power a product that is in no way competing with OpenAI fine? or is that Illegal as well?
author: jjmachan

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
Thanks for the question! We cannot provide legal advice. That said, our goal in DSP is to advance research into LLMs and not to compete with OpenAI.

For products, I can say two things:

First, OpenAI themselves have notebooks on how to train "curie" models on the output of Davinci: https://github.com/openai/openai-cookbook/blob/main/examples/fine-tuned_qa/olympics-3-train-qa.ipynb  —  You may consider whether you want to do something similar. Our compiler notebook trains an "ada" model. I think OpenAI will release more finetuning offerings very soon, which may be supported in our compiler.

Second, if you want to use a local open model, whether that qualifies as competing with OpenAI is (at most) unclear to me. Especially if the model you produce isn't the main service you're providing, but simply a component in your application. If you are to provide an API for your model as an LLM, then you're probably competing directly with OpenAI.

Again, none of this is legal advice. DSP is a research project. I hope these pointers help!

Okay, I've shared the following with another person who'd asked a couple of months ago.

The main thing not discussed below is that you need a ColBERTv2 index over the Wikipedia 2017 abstracts dataset from HotPotQA. Do you have this data/index? (You can't use the 2018 full index we're hosting if you want to do a reproduction; it's quite different. Also note that this isn't identical to the paper's runs, because the framework (v1) evolved a lot past what's discussed in the Dec 2022 paper. Lastly, you'll need to make sure to run this from v1 code even after we release v2 (later today!).

We'll maintain v1 on the `v1` branch on github.

1) Importing and setting up.

```
import dsp

davinci_002 = dsp.GPT3(model='text-davinci-002')
rm = dsp.ColBERTv2(port=2017, post_requests=True) # my colbert index of wiki 2017 abstracts

title: Does DSP can be used for entity extraction?
question_text:
Does DSP can be used for entity extraction?

In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), one of the most prominent problem statements is centered around Natural Language Search.
Suppose I possess a database with a predefined schema. When a user intends to formulate a query in natural language, my objective is to extract entity-value pairs from the query, thereby enabling the conversion of the natural language query into a structured query (such as SQL or Elasticsearch) that can be executed on the underlying database.
For instance, if my database contains a table with fields like "employee_name" and "job_description," and a user submits a query like "Joe with job description Software Developer," the desired outcome should be the extraction of entity-value pairs, such as employee_name: Joe and job_description: Software Developer, facilitating subsequent structured querying of the database.
Can this task be effectively accomplished within dsp framework.
Note: I have tried to use example in the repo, but unlike prompt technique where I can specify the output format, here in this case output are almost coming in passages with unrelated content. Tried to passed enough number of training examples as well.

Hi @mahmoudaymo ,

Following the `using_local_models.md` documentation should be particularly helpful from this [PR](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/pull/93/files#diff-77859fcc34f5a812c266e153cbbcd1ccd8d7ed5b07baddc468ba37b1be3538bd). 
The Text-Generation-Inference Server corresponds to using the HuggingFace models on the text-generation inference server supported by HuggingFace. 
HFModel corresponds to using the HF models locally.

More class-specific documentation can be found within `language_models_client.md` in the same [PR](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/pull/93/files#diff-458565a0ad7f388c1af1677e38eb16dc5321a4804511d91390fe8633fd6621c4)

Let me know if that helps or if you have any additional questions!

comments.author: okhat
comments.body: Thanks @mahmoudaymo ! @arnavsinghvi11 is looking into this

comments.author: arnavsinghvi11
comments.body:
Hi @mahmoudaymo 

You are correct in that `architectures` is not found in the [model config ](https://huggingface.co/TheBloke/Llama-2-7B-Chat-GGML/blob/main/config.json). 

I would actually suggest the following pivots to overcome this:
1. Using HFClientTGI over HFModel - the TGI server actually offers significant speed benefits and various other features like weight conversions, sharding, quantization, etc. that will make your runs much smoother compared to HFModel. 
2. Pivoting to the GPTQ format instead of GGML - TGI currently does not support [GGML formats ](https://github.com/huggingface/text-generation-inference/issues/909) but offers support for the GPTQ version of this model which you can use as per this [thread](https://github.com/huggingface/text-generation-inference/issues/920). (If using the GGML format is a strict requirement, I can do some more digging on how to support this within some other server frameworks we support). 

Some key notes to keep in mind:
-using the latest TGI docker  (`http://ghcr.io/huggingface/text-generation-inference:latest`) as our current docs mention using the 0.9.3 version but the latest version supports more advanced features and models (which we will eventually upgrade to as well)
-passing the `--quantize gptq` flag for the GPTQ format 
-referring to any other issues open on the TGI repo and/or additional relevant info on what other [GPTQ models are supported](https://github.com/huggingface/text-generation-inference/issues/601)

Please let me know if you have any additional questions!

Hey @jhyearsley !

Great question. This does seem confusing right now.

ColBERT is just a retriever. (It happens to be one that we built and one that we like, but that's all.)

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
The simplest explanation I wrote of DSPy was on HackerNews.

It said this:

You give DSPy (1) your free-form code with declarative calls to LMs, (2) a few inputs [labels optional], and (3) some validation metric [e.g., sanity checks].

It simulates your code on the inputs. When there's an LM call, it will make one or more simple zero-shot calls that respect your declarative signature. Think of this like a more general form of "function calling" if you will. It's just trying out things to see what passes your validation logic, but it's a highly-constrained search process.

The constraints enforced by the signature (per LM call) and the validation metric allow the compiler [with some metaprogramming tricks] to gather "good" and "bad" examples of execution for every step in which your code calls an LM. Even if you have no labels for it, because you're just exploring different pipelines. (Who has time to label each step?)

For now, we throw away the bad examples. The good examples become potential demonstrations. The compiler can now do an optimization process to find the best combination of these automatically bootstrapped demonstrations in the prompts. Maybe the best on average, maybe (in principle) the predicted best for a specific input. There's no magic here, it's just optimizing your metric.

The same bootstrapping logic lends itself (with more internal metaprogramming tricks, which you don't need to worry about) to finetuning models for your LM calls, instead of prompting.

In practice, this works really well because even tiny LMs can do powerful things when they see a few well-selected examples.

----

Does this sound useful?

comments.author: arnavsinghvi11
comments.body:
Hi 

Thank you for providing this example to reproduce! Couple of suggestions based on your use case:

Regarding "instead of answer I've got rationale instead of answer itself," I notice the MathSolverModule forward pass returns the predictor call itself (`self.generate_answer(**kwargs)`) which will indeed print out the Prediction object containing both rationale and answer. However, to meet your case of returning only answer, you would want to do `return dspy.Prediction(answer=prediction.answer)`. The RAG() module defined in the intro notebook is a great example for showing this!

Regarding the AttributeError you encounter, this was likely due to some internal conversion error between how the module is being serialized and somehow not retaining the Example object while being deserialized. A quick fix for this is including this snippet to override the update method of dsp.Example (`dspy/dsp/primitives/demonstrate.py` class Example) to fix the data format inconsistencies after the module is loaded:

```
def update(self, *args, **kwargs)

    super().update(*args, **kwargs)

    for key, value in self.items():

        if isinstance(value, dict) and not isinstance(value, Example):

            self[key] = Example(value)

        elif isinstance(value, list):

            self[key] = [Example(item) if isinstance(item, dict) and not isinstance(item, Example) else item for item in value]
```

However, this is something we will look further into as it seems to be a deeper bug in the loading of the saved module metadata correctly. Thank you for raising this error! Please let me know if you have any additional questions.

title: Multiple retriever's as tool use
question_text:
Multiple retriever's as tool use

Is it possible to use multiple retrievers/tools in the same RAG, where the right retriever is opted based on the prompt selection? Is this possible with DSPy? If so, could you please explain/add an example
author: dittops

comments.author: darinkishore
comments.body:
Take a look at the forward() method for your pipeline. 

psueodcode-ish: 
```python
Class ChooseBestRetriever(dspy.Module)

def __init__(self, retriever_params) # define all the things you want in your pipeline
    retriever_one = dspy.Retrieve() # set whatever retriever params you want here
    retriever_two = dspy.Retrieve() 
    retriever_three= = dspy.Retrieve()
    choose_retriever = dspy.MultiChainComparison("retriever 1 output, retriever 2 output, retriever 3 output -> best retriever")
    # other modules you need

def forward(self, input): # given input, how should we process it and turn it into the output we want?
    one_output = retriever_one(input)
    two_output = retriever_two(input)
    three_output = retriever_three(input)
    best_retriever = choose_retriever(one_output, two_output, three_output)
    # now that you have best retriever, figure out what to do with it
```

How do the retrievers differ? That informs how you use them in your pipeline. If they differ significantly, I'd suggest making different small DSPy programs for each retriever. 

The proper retriever choosing will be handled in the Teleprompter.compile() stage based on your metric you've chosen. I would suggest compiling examples for the input/output for determining best retriever for your current task. This will likely be difficult. You should be fine with 3-8 examples for train and dev set. 

The metric function will evaluate the results of this pipeline, and will be passed to teleprompter.compile() It should evaluate the choose_retriever. Think about how to evaluate if it's a good retriever based on the passages you get. This metric function may be complex, depending on how much you care. If you really want to have a good metric, use another DSPy program as the metric, possibly teleprompted on llama-2 or 3.5-turbo. You'd likely have to think about how you want that to be done as well. A simple metric, without creating another program, could be a hand-crafted GPT evaluation function, which will work okay and not cost too much because you probably don't have 500/0 examples ready to go.

title: How to make my own template in DSPy?
question_text:
How to make my own template in DSPy?

Hi,
I'm using DSPy with korean LM(this is in hugging face) and Retrieval.
But I'm having some problems in using it.
How can I rewrite template in Korean?
As I know there was Type and Template method in DSP but I couldn't find it in DSPy.
author: Chanwhistle

comments.author: detaos
comments.body:
On the surface, you can control most of the template by how you define your class:

For example, here's an "answer bot" that responds in Korean:

```
class AnswerInKorean(dspy.Signature):
    """Respond to the question in Korean"""
    
    question = dspy.InputField(
        prefix = "Question:",
        desc = "A question in English",
    )
    answer = dspy.OutputField(
        prefix="Answer:",
        desc="${the answer to the question, but only speak in Korean}"
    )

class AnswerBot(dspy.Module):
    def __init__(self, tools=None):
        super().__init__()

        self.generate_answer = dspy.ChainOfThought(AnswerInKorean)
        
    def forward(self, question):
        prediction = self.generate_answer(question=f"{question}")
        return dspy.Prediction(answer=prediction.answer)

uncompiled_answer_bot = AnswerBot()
pred = uncompiled_answer_bot(question="What's the weahter like over there?")
print(pred.answer)
```

> 저기 날씨가 어때요.

You can see the prompt by doing this:
```
lm.inspect_history(n=1)
```
```
Respond to the question in Korean

---

Strictly adhere to the following format:

Question: A question in English
Reasoning: Let's think step by step in order to ${produce the answer}. We ...
Answer: ${the answer to the question, but only speak in Korean}

---

Question: What's the weather like over there?
Reasoning: Let's think step by step in order to 저기 날씨가 어때요? We need to translate the question into Korean, so we can ask it to someone who speaks Korean. To do this, we need to know the Korean words for "what's the weather like" and "over there". In Korean, "what's the weather like" is "날씨가 어때요" and "over there" can be translated as "저기". So, we put these two phrases together to get "저기 날씨가 어때요".
Answer: 저기 날씨가 어때요.
```

You can see I also changed the usual "Follow the following format" to "Strictly adhere to the following format".  That was done by editing `dsp/templates/template_v2.py`.

To modify the Chain of Thought prefix, you can make your own type and pass it to the CoT constructor.  In `AnswerBot`'s `__init__`:

```
    cot_type = dsp.Type(
        prefix="Reasoning: Let's think step by step in order to",
        desc="${produce the answer}. We ..."
    )
    self.generate_answer = dspy.ChainOfThought(AnswerInKorean, rationale_type=cot_type)
```
(Be sure to `import dsp` if you want to make your own type.)

title: Support for Chat-Completion model APIs
question_text:
Support for Chat-Completion model APIs

The "chat-completion-API" where a model receives a `system prompt` and a list of `messages` assigned to different `roles` is gaining traction. OpenAI's chat API is driven by this interaction-model, but other open source models implement the same interaction-model (e.g. Llama2 or openchat-3.5).
Currently, the OpenAI binding in dspy packs signatures and (few-shot) examples into one prompt string and sends it to OpenAI as a `user` message (https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/main/dsp/modules/gpt3.py#L87).
This simplified approach has drawbacks because the natural mapping of `signature` -> `system prompt`, `inputs` -> `user message` and `outputs` -> `assistant message` is lost. GPT-4 might be less brittle to this unorthodox use of user messages, but the performance of open source models degrade a lot when the expected format is not used.
The `HFClientVLLM` binding currently doesn't support the chat-completion API.
Instead of packing everything into one `user message`, dspy should map signature docstrings to `system prompts`, inputs to `user messages` and outputs to `assistant messages` to make ideal usage of the underlying models' capabilities.

title: Implement FunSearch in DSPy
question_text:
Implement FunSearch in DSPy

A [recent paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06924-6) by DeepMind demonstrated the use of FunSearch, an "evolutionary procedure" pairing an LLM with a systematic evaluator, on problems in extremal combinatorics (cap set) and algorithm design (online bin packing). The paper, while excellent and containing interesting work, went viral due to sensational media positioning such as: "[DeepMind AI outdoes human mathematicians on unsolved problem](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-04043-w)" and the resulting (predictable) AGI/ASI grifting.
While reading this paper I couldn't help but think of DSPy. I continue to believe this framework is "skating to where the puck will be" in terms of building truly useful, trustworthy, maintainable, LM-based systems, at least until a dramatic breakthrough in LM capabilities (e.g. reasoning, world model, etc.). It recognizes the inherent variability/unreliability and limitations of LMs today and provides useful guardrails around them in production systems. This was further enhanced with Suggest and Assert. It also enables us to take advantage of the LM's ability to generate novel solutions or approaches - a core element of FunSearch.
I suspect replicating FunSearch in DSPy would enable it to address an even larger class of real-world scientific and business problems. As I understand it there are at least three areas which may require additional research/development to implement FunSearch (red in diagram):
- Signatures would need the ability to use an “immutable” prompt “skeleton”. This is how DeepMind handled it at least, with a simple part of the prompt (a subset of the Python code called the “program”) being varied in each prompt.
- We would need to dust off dspy.PythonInterpreter to execute the latest code variants.
- Assuming my diagram is directionally correct, I'm unsure if the teleprompter is where we would want to execute and score each variant and then persist the “program” along with its evaluation score. We would perhaps then implement our genetic algorithm / island strategy as a retriever to select the example "programs" to include from the module, but someone could tell me this belongs in teleprompter as well.
![dspy_flowchart](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/assets/32801342/fac42838-5b6d-4e44-91dd-e2aa935bb9bf)
I’ll share additional thoughts as I proceed. I only recently dove into the DSPy code base, so any feedback from the community on my understanding (or lack thereof) and guidance on research would be greatly appreciated!
author: mattredlon

comments.author: darinkishore
comments.body:
@mattredlon 

Spitballing, but take a look at this issue/PR combo. Would this be what you were thinking about for item 1? (Signatures would need the ability to use an “immutable” prompt “skeleton”.)

https://github.com/darinkishore/dspy/issues/68

https://github.com/darinkishore/dspy/pull/69

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
Hey @mattredlon,

> teleprompter is where we would want to execute and score each variant and then persist the “program” along with its evaluation score. We would perhaps then implement our genetic algorithm / island strategy as a retriever to select the example "programs" to include from the module, but someone could tell me this belongs in teleprompter as well.

With the big caveat that I (i) read your post carefully (ii) never read the FunSearch paper or any content about it yet unfortunately, I think this all belongs in a new teleprompter.

We'll rename teleprompters to optimizers so let me start using that term now. Basically I can imagine a `dspy.optimize.FunSearch` optimizer. It will take `FunSearch(**general_config_and_hyperparams)` and will have `.compile(program, trainset`) as usual.

In terms of the original design, Signatures in DSPy are stateless and immutable.* The optimized parts are held inside the modules, basically/mainly dspy.Predict. (Other modules generally use dspy.Predict in different ways.)

The main things that can be optimized are typically instructions and demonstrations (or the LM weights if we're finetuning). I assume FunSearch is more about the instructions?

Footnote: Even I think eventually signatures should be stateless and immutable in principle, we took some shortcuts in SignatureOptimizer where it *does* mutate the instruction of the signature. Probably not the right long-term thing to do.

Json Support

Is it possible to use json objects for context and answers?
Is the best solution to do something like:
[code]
Or some other JSON Schema.
author: thomasahle

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
Hey @thomasahle. In typical usage, the Signature itself serves as the schema. That is, you can request multiple output fields (e.g., summary and commands) for your structure.

Here's one example:
```python
class ExampleSignature(dspy.Signature):
    question = dspy.InputField()
    summary = dspy.OutputField()
    json = dspy.OutputField(desc='key-value pairs')

generate = dspy.Predict(ExampleSignature)
response = generate(question="What are the acronyms of west-coast US states?")
```

Here, response is:
```
Prediction(
    summary='The acronyms of west-coast US states are CA (California), OR (Oregon), and WA (Washington).',
    json='{\n  "CA": "California",\n  "OR": "Oregon",\n  "WA": "Washington"\n}'
)
```

This is zero-shot usage, which is not most reliable. Generally, you'd then do one of two things:
- Compile on a few examples to optimize the prompt so it does whatever you need more reliably. Usually, your goal isn't just valid JSON but also useful values in the JSON outputs (i.e., correct semantically and syntactically).
- Use `dspy.Suggest` with criteria for valid JSON fitting your schema, if any. This will retry if there are failures and has the capacity to optimize the prompt selection during compiling. [Read more here about DSPy assertions.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.13382)

That said, if your goal is explicitly to generate valid JSON, we are lacking on solid guidance and tooling for that. I think Outlines has the right answers there (though I suspect we can optimize cost-wise) and could serve as a great backend for structured outputs in DSPy.

title: Does metric have to return `bool`?
question_text:
Does metric have to return `bool`?

I am thinking about writing a program for a "batch processing" task, i.e., each call to the program, there will be a list of inputs, and the output is a corresponding list for the inputs. To optimize such a program, a natural metric would be something like "out of the 20 inputs, how many of them are correctly answered?".
I think in this case, I probably need a numerical metric instead of bool metric. Is that right? If so, do you think it is good to extend metric for this?
Thanks!
author: breakds

comments.author: okhat
comments.body: You can return a float score!

comments.author: okhat
comments.body: Yeah this only affects how few shot examples are created. It doesn’t affect anything else!

comments.author: grand-cat-unknown
okhat
comments.body:
Sorry I'm adding material about this to the docs.

There's a couple of examples of this, here's one: https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/main/examples/tweets/tweet_metric.py

```python
def metric(gold, pred, trace=None):
    question, answer, tweet = gold.question, gold.answer, pred.output
    context = retrieve(question).passages

    engaging = "Does the assessed text make for a self-contained, engaging tweet?"
    faithful = "Is the assessed text grounded in the context? Say no if it includes significant facts not in the context."
    correct = f"The text above is should answer `{question}`. The gold answer is `{answer}`."
    correct = f"{correct} Does the assessed text above contain the gold answer?"
    
    with dspy.context(lm=gpt4T):
        faithful = dspy.Predict(Assess)(context=context, assessed_text=tweet, assessment_question=faithful)
        correct =  dspy.Predict(Assess)(context='N/A', assessed_text=tweet, assessment_question=correct)
        engaging = dspy.Predict(Assess)(context='N/A', assessed_text=tweet, assessment_question=engaging)

    correct, engaging, faithful = [m.assessment_answer.lower() == 'yes' for m in [correct, engaging, faithful]]
    score = (correct + engaging + faithful) if correct and (len(tweet) <= 280) else 0

    if trace is not None: return score >= 3
    return score / 3.0
```

The last two lines are what matters.

Basically:

1. If `trace` is `None` (i.e., if we're *not* creating few-shot examples), it returns a float, in this case `score / 3.0`. It doesn't have to be out between 0.0 and 1.0 but it's nice for your own sanity. This is a `float` because, during optimization or evaluation, we want to find the average score overall.
2. Otherwise (i.e., if we *are* creating few-shot examples), it returns a `bool` with a threshold (`score >= 3`). This is a `bool` because we need to know whether or not this example is, ultimately, worthy of using as a demonstration.

Does this make sense?

One note: `trace` is the variable of the full trace of the DSPy program, which is given to your metric during bootstrapping new examples so you can "look back" at all inputs and outputs of all steps of the program. Here, we're just checking if `trace` is set. If it's `None`, it means we're either optimizing or evaluating, but not bootstrapping.

@okhat  It seems that not all available OpenAI API SDK endpoints are compatible with all the default args we have set in GPT3. Should we refactor the default [kwargs](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/df8372acf29270f88f8c8961f80bc010b574e576/dsp/modules/gpt3.py#L97) only to include `temperature` and `max_tokens` potentially, and leave the rest as configurable by the user?

comments.author: JLKaretis
comments.body:
I've had some success using a custom class like this, for Mistral models deployed with Azure. This isn't fully tested, results might vary

`from mistralai.client import MistralClient
from mistralai.models.chat_completion import ChatMessage
import os
from dsp import LM
from typing import Any

class Mistral(LM):

    def __init__(self, model, api_key, endpoint, **kwargs):
        self.model = model
        self.api_key = api_key
        self.endpoint = endpoint 
        self.client = MistralClient(endpoint=self.endpoint, api_key=self.api_key)
        self.kwargs = {
            "temperature": 0.0,
            "max_tokens": 150,
            "top_p": 1,
            "frequency_penalty": 0,
            "presence_penalty": 0,
            "n": 1,
            **kwargs,
        }
        self.history: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
        self.provider = "openai"

    def basic_request(self, prompt: str, **kwargs):
        chat_response = self.client.chat(
            model=self.model,
            messages=[
                ChatMessage(role="user", content=prompt)
            ],
            **kwargs
        )
        response_dict = json.loads(chat_response.model_dump_json())

        self.history.append({
            "prompt": prompt,
            "response": response_dict, #{"choices": chat_response.choices[0].message.content},
            "kwargs": kwargs,
        })

        return chat_response

    def __call__(self, prompt, only_completed=True, return_sorted=False, **kwargs):
        response = self.request(prompt, **kwargs)
        completions = [response.choices[0].message.content] 
        return completions
    
    def _get_choice_text(self, choice: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
        
        return choice["message"]["content"]`

author: Josephrp

comments.author: kylebarone
comments.body: @Josephrp Do you have any example papers or literature on the biases with LLM evaluators? Also do you have any good key-words or links to start looking for appropriate evaluator models?

comments.author: Joshmantova
comments.body:
Do we want to use hosted endpoints that already exist within prebuilt spaces or do we want to curate a list of HF models and support custom-built endpoints based on those? I'd recommend supporting custom-built endpoints rather than existing spaces to support enterprise use cases. Additionally, I'd be concerned about the reliability of existing spaces.

I don't see any examples of adaters in `dspy/adapter` - how do we envision adapters being integrated? Should this not be implemented in `dsp/modules`?

Here are a list of potential models I've identified that might be helpful for this use case. A great starting point would be to identify models to generate each metric within the [RAGAS](https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/index.html) testing framework. Note that I have not tried any of these models but I think models that solve some of these tasks might be useful for this issue's use case.
* [Hallucination eval](https://huggingface.co/vectara/hallucination_evaluation_model)
* [Relevance eval](https://huggingface.co/mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v1)
* [Toxicity](https://huggingface.co/s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier)
* [Fact / opinion classifier](https://huggingface.co/lighteternal/fact-or-opinion-xlmr-el)
* [Bias detection](https://huggingface.co/d4data/bias-detection-model)
* [Sentiment](https://huggingface.co/nam194/sentiment)
* [NSFW detection](https://huggingface.co/qiuhuachuan/NSFW-detector)
* [Programming language classification](https://huggingface.co/philomath-1209/programming-language-identification)
* [Faithfulness classifier](https://huggingface.co/CogComp/bart-faithful-summary-detector)
* [Grammar / correctness / completeness classifier](https://huggingface.co/Ashishkr/query_wellformedness_score)

I'd love some feedback on these questions / this approach. If it's along the lines of what the team is envisioning, I might have time to take a shot at a PR to implement this.

comments.author: Joshmantova
comments.body:
A couple of notes about implementation:
* It looks like the current HF client is built for local models - not models from HF endpoints
* We should create a provider to make calls to HF endpoints (or just hijack one of the other providers and provide a custom URL)
* We should then create an abstract HF adapter that allows users to specify a model name, and anything else that substantially differs between models, and allows users to easily make calls to HF endpoints. This should also follow practices outlined in DSPy such as implementing or piggybacking off of an existing `inspect_history` method.
* Then we can just create adapters for each model that allows users to import that adapter and use it like they would any other model without having to worry about the endpoint calling implementation. This would allow users to see a curated list of models and use them easily.

Open questions:
* Do these HF models require us to call them very differently?
* Do we want to automatically create the custom endpoint for the user or do we want to assume they have created it in their HF account?
* Is the existing HF model too specifically built for local models or can we refactor it to be used in both remote and local use cases?
* How do we want to handle rate limits and token limits?
* Are these selected models high enough quality for us to firmly recommend to the community? Should we instead create DSPy models using GPT4 that assess each of the selected metrics rather than relying on a HF model for each? That's probably what I'd do first if this was something I wanted to do in my use case.

Once we clear up these open questions, implementation should be easy. Do you guys want to help look into these open questions?

def generate_qa(context: str, n_qa_pairs: int = 5) -> list:

query = query_generator(context=context, config=dict(temperature=0.7 + (0.1 * i)))

title: Adding integrated planner algorithms functionality?
question_text:
Adding integrated planner algorithms functionality?

Would that be in scope? If we can write some templates to force llm to describe the problem space, we could run a [planning algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_planning_and_scheduling) to solve tasks in that space. The big issue with planners back in the day was that you had to manually specify the problem space.
The benefits would be
1. Much faster execution.
2. Actual alignment. Right now user's llm can be jailbroken, for example by using ASCII art.
3. Interpretability. If you use llm to just describe things, and then planner takes over, you get debug info for free.
4. Significantly improved programmability. A functional integrated planner could make fuzzy programming over general text possible. If llm can pars and define actors for your program you can do the rest in a generic way.
5. Caching. If llm just breaks down the problem space you can reuse that breakdown.
I'm not aware of anyone doing this, but it seems like a good opposite to "7 trillion dollars to train a gigantic blackbox" that the api providers are doing.

title: Support Chat Mode
question_text: Support Chat Mode Hopefully the new LM backend will allow us to make better use of models that are trained for "Chat". Below is a good example of how even good models like GPT-3.5 are currently have trouble understanding the basic DSPy format: Right now we use chat mode as if it was completion mode. We send: [code] And expect the agent to reply with [code] A better use of the Chat APIs would be to send [code] That is, we simulate a previous chat, where the agent always replied with the output in the format we expect. This teaches the agent to not start it's message with "OK! Let me get to it!" or repeating the template as in the gpt-3.5 screenshot above. Also, using the system message for the guidance should help avoid prompt injection attacks.
author: thomasahle

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
Totally agreed but I'd love for this to be more data-driven.

Either: (a) meta prompt engineering for popular models + easy addition of new adapters for new LMs if needed, or (b) automatic exploration of a new LM on standard tasks to automatically establish the patterns that "work" for that LM.

Do you have a way that fixes the sql_query example you had?

comments.author: okhat
comments.body: Also I wonder to what extent this behavior you saw is because of "Follow the following format." is not explicitly saying "Complete the unfilled fields in accordance with the following format." Basically the instruction is slightly misleading for chat models.

comments.author: CyrusNuevoDia
comments.body:
My sense is that interleaving inputs/outputs as a default would be a footgun because I would assume all outputs depend on all inputs, and the LLM doesn’t have access to this. 

Right now our focus is using LiteLLM for broad support + moving over all dsp code into DSPy. 

I’d love to tackle something like this when we look at the current Template usage and how that’s currently responsible for going from Example => prompt, and offering users some more flexibility with how an LLM gets called with an example.

comments.author: meditans
comments.body:
I feel the problem with this is most of the time the positioning of the user end token. Say you have a prompt template that wraps the user message in `[INST]` and `[/INST]`, like in `mixtral`. You would have:

```
[INST]
...

input1: ...
input2: ...
output:[/INST]

???
```
It seems to me that the model is lead to believe that the user turn is done (and the user has written a complete template, albeit with an empty output). It would be more correct to say:

```
[INST]
...

input1: ...
input2: ...[/INST]

output: ???
```

explicitly leaving the output field to the assistant (it suffices to create a `{"role": "assistant", "content":"output:"}` message).




> Also I wonder to what extent this behavior you saw is because of "Follow the following format." is not explicitly saying "Complete the unfilled fields in accordance with the following format." Basically the instruction is slightly misleading for chat models.

@okhat I have done this experiment by writing a mini-version of `Predict` myself, with the prompt you are suggesting. I still have the same problem @thomasahle demonstrated in his initial post. This reinforces for me the belief that the token position is to blame. The version I proposed works instead.

> Totally agreed but I'd love for this to be more data-driven.

I don't know precisely what you have in mind, but it seems to me that fixing the semantic of the multi-turn user-assistant conversation is orthogonal to the concern of wording the prompt differently.

comments.body:
@thomasahle you are right, I am using a (local, quantized) chat finetune of mixtral, not baseline mixtral.

question_text:
TypedPredictor asking for 'very succinct' object leads to incomplete object in output

When a typed predictor creates examples, it uses the following promt [here](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/7227e7081d8edc3d0ffc2729f7c97871aa61338b/dspy/functional/functional.py#L103), which states:
This is problematic. In my case I have a quite complex schema with many fields, a few of which are nested. Sometimes the prompt works, but often the object that's output is missing required fields. I think the root cause is that the example that's created by that prompt is also missing fields.
Note that it seems the model (GPT4) is aware of this. Beneath the LLM-generated example, the model notes that

author: arunpatro

comments.author: arnavsinghvi11
comments.body:
Hi @arunpatro, I believe 

```
class AssertReason(BaseModel):
    assertion: str = Field()
    reason: str = Field()
    answer: Literal["A", "B", "C", "D"] = Field()
```

should not have the type declarations here since it inherits from `BaseModel`, not `Signature` which has `dspy.InputField` and `dspy.OutputField`. 

```
class AssertReason(BaseModel):
    assertion: str
    reason: str
    answer: Literal["A", "B", "C", "D"]
```

Let me know if that fixes it or any others follow up.

Feel free to reference documentation on [Functional types in DSPy](https://dspy-docs.vercel.app/api/category/functional)!

comments.author: MarkusOdenthal
comments.body:
Hi @arunpatro. I had the same problem and figured out how to implement this. Try this:

```
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field 
from typing import Literal, List
from dspy.functional import TypedPredictor
from dspy import Signature, InputField, OutputField

class AssertReason(BaseModel):
      assertion: str = Field()
      reason: str = Field()
      answer: List[Literal["A", "B", "C", "D"]] = Field()
    
class AssertReasonDSPy(Signature):
    """ Generate a list of assertions and reasons for the given context."""
    context: str = InputField()
    items: AssertReason = OutputField()

predictor = TypedPredictor(AssertReasonDSPy)
text = "Coffee One day around 850 CE, a goat herd named Kaldi observed that, after nibbling on some berries, his goats started acting abnormally. Kaldi tried them himself, and soon enough, he was just as hyper. This was humanity's first run-in with coffee— or so the story goes."
predictor(context=text)
```

comments.author: tkellogg
comments.body:
All this is great, but I want to add a couple additional items:

1. Watch `max_tokens`, I know that OllamaLocal defaults it to 150
    ```python
    ollama_model = dspy.OllamaLocal(
        model="llama3.1",
        model_type="instruct",
        format="json",
        max_tokens=20000,
    )
    ```
2. The schema can get so complex that the LLM needs optimization just to get off the ground. To fix this, skip validation on parts of the model. 
    ```python
    class AssertReason(BaseModel):
      assertion: str = Field()
      reason: str = Field()
      answer: List[pydantic.SkipValidation[Literal["A", "B", "C", "D"]]] = Field()
    ````

I wish there were some configurability in how JSON is parsed. I'd love to handle invalid JSON  specially. If the JSON gets cut off due to the `max_tokens`, then either you want to raise that or maybe chunk your text. Either way, there's almost zero operational visibility into what's going on. No bueno.

title: Would suggest COPRO ignore "return_outputs"

comments.author: arnavsinghvi11
comments.body:
Hi @oekekezie , thanks for raising this issue. 

I believe this is because `return_outputs` returns a tuple of the evaluation score and a list of outputs with Example types (which is handled in various conditions within Evaluate [here](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/696f2d2e1f96f173abb36302c71a725d564dfadb/dspy/evaluate/evaluate.py#L228))

lmk if this is indeed the issue and if adding that condition within COPRO handles it. Feel free to push a PR for it if so or share your program and stack trace so we can take a closer look. Thanks again for finding this!

title: Is there a generic way to change model's `max_tokens` dynamically?
question_text:
Is there a generic way to change model's `max_tokens` dynamically?

I have a use case where I want to use the same LM in different steps with different `max_tokens` and context size. I use `dspy.configure` to set this LM.
Some of my steps will require much shorter output, so it would be useful to do something like this:
[code]
Is it currently possible to simulate this? If yes, how can I specify pass this to lm's `kwargs`?
Obviously one could do this by resetting `dspy.context(lm=...)` but it would be pretty cumbersome, it also seems for me that the point of `dspy.configure` to set LM is that the modules should abstract over what LM is actually used (but setting a key parameter like the context length or number of generated tokens seems reasonable).
author: lambdaofgod

comments.author: kylerush
comments.body:
I believe there is a [context manager](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/issues/168#issuecomment-1763406841) for this.

```python
with dspy.settings.context(max_tokens=32):
    result = module1(first_input)

with dspy.settings.context(max_tokens=128):
   result = module2(first_input)
```

comments.author: arnavsinghvi11
comments.body:
@lambdaofgod  you can set the LM per step through the context manager and dynamically change the respective LM's tokens as needed:

```
with dspy.context(lm=dspy.OpenAI(...., max_tokens= x)):
  ....
with dspy.context(lm=dspy.OpenAI(...., max_tokens= x+1)):
  ....

```

comments.author: arnavsinghvi11
comments.body:
@lambdaofgod would `dspy.settings.config['lm'].kwargs['max_tokens'] = ..` cover the abstraction here?

you wouldn't have to expose the defined lm and can still wrap modules using `with dspy.context(lm = lm)`

```
lm = dspy.OpenAI(model=..., max_tokens=32)

dspy.settings.configure(lm=lm)

with dspy.settings.context(lm= lm):
    result = module1(first_input)

dspy.settings.config['lm'].kwargs['max_tokens'] = 128

with dspy.settings.context(lm= lm):
   result = module2(first_input)
```

comments.author: arnavsinghvi11
comments.body: @lambdaofgod They are quite similar, just that the reference I provided is already built in with DSPy and wouldn't require any additional changes :).

comments.body: Makes sense @lambdaofgod . Feel free to push a PR that can better handle this behavior in `dspy.context` without impacting existing settings!

I want to generate only the answer, not the `tokens`
author: dhilst

comments.author: gidler
comments.body:
The `Follow the following format` comes from [this line](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/66573d66622acd73e8bfe68a6c098a5351826db2/dsp/templates/template_v2.py#L121) in the default `Template`, which is used by `Predict`. I don't see a way around it if you are using `Predict` in your Module/Pipeline.

You can prompt engineer your way into only getting "Yes" or "No" in your answer. For example, I did it with:
```

title: Support for batching for LM clients (OpenAI, vLLM etc)
question_text:
Support for batching for LM clients (OpenAI, vLLM etc)

I have seen conversations where it has been mentioned that Evaluate has `num_threads` parameters that can parallelize but I am not completely sure if it provides significant performance gains compared to batching.
Reasoning:
* Python doesn't truly support multi-threading.
* Bottleneck in performance is sending data over to the GPU.
Solution:
* Send a batch of data even when running the dspy.Predict()
For example:
[code]
author: AmoghM

comments.author: mikeedjones
comments.body:
The main blocker to this change would be that [graph compilation is not supported for `n>1`](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/b05394bb20722444648a33b4447156bcef202fd6/dsp/primitives/predict.py#L157) - however, I'm not sure what you mean exactly in this case that python doesn't support multi-threading, and the bottleneck is sending data to the GPU? 

In your example, the loading of the tokens into gpu memory is handled by the huggingface client on `localhost:8000` - which has nothing to do with dspy or the process in which dspy is running. I'm not sure that sending the prompts across to that port is the bottleneck in performance? In any case, [vllm supports continuous batching](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/index.html#welcome-to-vllm:~:text=Continuous%20batching%20of%20incoming%20requests) so the batch size for the actual inference (and any sending of data across to the GPU) will be determined by vLLM based on a whole host of things. 

As for threadpool executors - which is how dspy runs multiple `Predict`s at once - [its probably the best choice for sending off a bunch of concurrent http requests](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html#threadpoolexecutor-example) as dspy does. The polling overhead is pretty insubstantial when compared to inference time and `num_threads` is not likely to get anywhere near the sorts of numbers where it could become a problem.

comments.author: okhat
comments.body: Thank you @AmoghM , @mikeedjones ! We don't plan to add batching. But we will add utilities for easier parallelism. Multi-threading is actually perfectly fine since the bottleneck is always on the server not the client.

title: Triton Inference Server
question_text:
Triton Inference Server

When it comes to fully production grade inference servers, TIS is very much optimized and open sourced. So an integration of this in dspy along with trt llm (#1094) would be some great additions.
author: Anindyadeep

comments.author: this-josh
comments.body:
It needs to be tidied up for a PR, but here is a working example of using Triton with dspy

```python
import numpy as np
import tritonclient.grpc as grpcclient
from tritonclient.utils import np_to_triton_dtype
import threading
from dsp.modules.lm import LM

class TritonLMClient(LM):
    def __init__(self, url, model, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(model,**kwargs)
        self.client = grpcclient.InferenceServerClient(url=url)
        self.model = model
        self.kwargs = {
            "temperature": 0.7,  # Default temperature
            "max_tokens": 2048,  # Default max tokens
        }
        self.provider ='tensorrt_llm'
    
    def generate(self, prompt, **kwargs):
        # Update kwargs with any provided parameters
        self.kwargs.update(kwargs)
        result_event = threading.Event()
        output_result = None

        
        # Prepare the input
        input_data = np.array([[prompt.encode()]], dtype=object)  # Changed to 2D array
        max_tokens = np.array([[self.kwargs['max_tokens']]], dtype=np.int32)  # Already 2D array
        temperature = np.array([[self.kwargs['temperature']]], dtype=np.float32)  # Already 2D array
        inputs = [
            grpcclient.InferInput("text_input", input_data.shape, np_to_triton_dtype(input_data.dtype)),
            grpcclient.InferInput("max_tokens", max_tokens.shape, np_to_triton_dtype(max_tokens.dtype)),
            grpcclient.InferInput("temperature", temperature.shape, np_to_triton_dtype(temperature.dtype)),
        ]
        inputs[0].set_data_from_numpy(input_data)
        inputs[1].set_data_from_numpy(max_tokens)
        inputs[2].set_data_from_numpy(temperature)
        # Prepare the output
        outputs = [
            grpcclient.InferRequestedOutput("text_output")
        ]

        def callback_function(result, error):
            nonlocal output_result

            if error:
                raise Exception(f"Received error: {error}")

            output = result.as_numpy("text_output")
            if output.dtype.type is np.bytes_:
                output_text = output.item().decode('utf-8')
            else:
                output_text = str(output)
            output_result= output_text
            result_event.set()

        self.client.start_stream(callback=callback_function)

        self.client.async_stream_infer(model_name=self.model, inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)
        result_event.wait(timeout=10)

title: Modifying optimized prompt in dspy.Predict
question_text:
Modifying optimized prompt in dspy.Predict

Is there a way to modify the optimized prompt used by a dspy program?
I am using dspy for a classification task where I am providing the list of classes to choose from. However, the list of classes is large (1000 classes), and the optimized prompt for chatgpt 3.5/4 uses few-shot learning, and so the list of classes is repeated in the prompt multiple times. This is a problem due to the rate limit of the gpt models. I want to modify the prompt, i.e: submit custom prompt where I only provide the list of classes once.
author: anas-elgamma

comments.author: tom-doerr
comments.body:
You could just use a signature class and add the classes to the description:
```
class GenerateSearchQuery(dspy.Signature):
    """Write a simple search query that will help answer a complex question."""

    context = dspy.InputField(desc="may contain relevant facts")
    question = dspy.InputField()
    query = dspy.OutputField()
```
Prompt:
```
Write a simple search query that will help answer a complex question.

---

Follow the following format.

Context: may contain relevant facts

Question: ${question}

Reasoning: Let's think step by step in order to ${produce the query}. We ...

Query: ${query}

---

Context: N/A

Question: In what year was the club founded that played Manchester City in the 1972 FA Charity Shield

Reasoning: Let's think step by step in order to produce the query. We know that the FA Charity Shield is an annual football match played in England between the winners of the previous season's Premier League and FA Cup. In this case, we are looking for the year when Manchester City played against a specific club in the 1972 FA Charity Shield. To find this information, we can search for the history of the FA Charity Shield and the teams that participated in the 1972 edition.

Query: "History of FA Charity Shield 1972"

---

Context: N/A

Question: Which is taller, the Empire State Building or the Bank of America Tower?

Reasoning: Let's think step by step in order to produce the query. We need to find the heights of both buildings and compare them.

Query: "height of Empire State Building" OR "height of Bank of America Tower"

---

Context: N/A

Question: Who is older, Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov or Anatoly Fomenko?

Reasoning: Let's think step by step in order to produce the query. We can search for the birth dates of both Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov and Anatoly Fomenko and compare them to determine who is older.

Query: "Birth date Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov" "Birth date Anatoly Fomenko"

```

Alternatively you could use a retriever

comments.author: thickett
comments.body:
do you mean that you want the agent to do the function calling? if so this is quite simple;

Function calling can be achieved using tools that you can define within the DSPY framework. 

you can read about it [here](https://dspy-docs.vercel.app/docs/deep-dive/modules/react#react-tools): 

it is rather simple; 
1. define your python functions, which can quite literaly do anything, and can take input parameters that are generated as part of your agent, i.e you can have the LLM generate inputs, feed user-inputs through etc. 

2. create a toolbox

3. supply this toolbox to the ReAct module, you can either use this with the default signature, or of course create your own specific for your task.

4. you can then simply use this as a building block in your program, add suggest/assert statements etc as you would do with any other dspy program.


here is an example of defining some basic tools to give a general idea of how you would create a module for function calling:

`
```

from openai import OpenAI
from dsp import LM
from datetime import datetime

from typing import Any, Dict
import dspy
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from ast import literal_eval

from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()


class OpenAICompatible(LM):
    def __init__(
            self,
            model: str,
            api_key: str,
            base_url: str,
            **kwargs
    ):
        super().__init__(model=model)
        self.base_url = base_url
        self.api_key = api_key
        self.model = model
        self.kwargs.update(kwargs)

    def basic_request(self, prompt, **kwargs):
        config = dict()
        config.update(self.kwargs)
        config['model'] = self.model
        config.update(kwargs)

        messages = [
            {
                "role": "system",
                "content": "You are a helpful assistant."
            },
            {
                'role': 'user',
                'content': prompt
            }
        ]

        client = OpenAI(
            api_key=self.api_key,
            base_url=self.base_url
        )

        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            messages=messages,
            **config,
        )

        self.history.append({
            'prompt': prompt,
            'response': response,
            'kwargs': config,
        })

        return response

    def get_choice_text(self, choice: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
        message = choice.message
        content = message.content
        if message.tool_calls != None:
            return str([
                {
                    'name': tool.function.name,
                    'arguments': tool.function.arguments
                } for tool in message.tool_calls])
        return content

    def __call__(self, prompt, only_completed=True, return_sorted=False, **kwargs):
        response = self.request(prompt, **kwargs)

        completions = [self.get_choice_text(choice)
                       for choice in response.choices]

        return completions

When using a metric that can be higher than 1, evaluate can produce logs like "Average Metric: 49 / 10"

Maybe for now the docs should mention that scores should be normalised between 0 and 1?

title: Support for setting OpenAI project field in addition to api_key? (I would be happy to send PR; not requesting work from team)
question_text:
Support for setting OpenAI project field in addition to api_key? (I would be happy to send PR; not requesting work from team)

Hello,
Thanks for a great project.
In https://platform.openai.com/settings/ , OpenAI allows the configuration (API keys, rate limits, usage, and allowed models, etc) to be grouped by Projects, which have IDs.
![Screenshot_20240919_132005](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a6bfcb69-7732-4322-ac66-1392fd252b9e)
The current DSPy OpenAI adapter `dsp/modules/gpt3.py`
(named gpt3.py but supports many OpenAI models like gpt4, and even o-1 as of https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/928068e866a9d13c42cefa851871841c42e6b5fb )
obviously allows passing one's API key when instantiating it:
https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/2cc029b03e18fe3bc05b5131ef3e02390af895b3/dsp/modules/gpt3.py#L59
However, DSPy's OpenAI adapter does not currently seem to allow specifying a particular project. One can use project specific API keys to work around this pretty easily but it also just a couple of lines code change to allow picking up a project argument from the `kwargs`, something like:
[code]
added right AFTER `self.kwargs` is defined in `__init__` at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/2cc029b03e18fe3bc05b5131ef3e02390af895b3/dsp/modules/gpt3.py#L98
will do the trick (tested and verified by me).
![add_project_support_manually](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ed8efc57-d9ae-41ba-9e24-45c9c52e59b2)
Any interest in a quick PR from me (or your team if preferred) to allow users who have a single multi-project API key to specify which project their DSPy activity in that particular code execution should be tracked against?
Thanks again for an awesome project!
(Credit to Stanford XCS224U for introducing me to DSPy)

hi @willy-b , litellm indeed doesn't support the project parameter currently either, but maybe we can get by this by setting the openai configurable parameters before the LM call, rather than within the request?

```
import openai
openai.api_key = '...'
openai.project = "..."

lm = dspy.LM(model=model, ...)
```

a bit of a patchy solution, but it'll probably be easier than adding any new parameters for future OpenAI API changes. lmk if that helps!

title: How to constrain the number of few shot examples ?
question_text:
How to constrain the number of few shot examples ?

Hi @stanfordnlp, thank you very much for your works!
I am using the MIPROv2 teleprompter to jointly optimize both instruction and few shot sets. In my use case, I need to compare MIPROv2 with other prompting methods. For fair comparison, we set an equal budget for each method (max 3 exemplars). As far as I understand, setting the parameter `max_labeled_demos` would equal to the size of the exemplar set. However, when I tried running, the final demos usually contain more examples (I was setting `max_bootstrapped_demos=10, max_labeled_demos=3`, but usually get `4` to `8` examples). I think I misunderstood somehow, could you help me in this ?
cc @okhat @arnavsinghvi11 @krypticmouse @isaacbmiller @thomasahle @CShorten (sorry if I tagged the wrong person)
author: thangld201

comments.author: okhat
comments.body: You can set max_labeled_demos=3 and max_bootstrapped_demos=3.

comments.author: CShorten
comments.body:
Hey @thangld201, the `max_bootstrapped_demos` argument refers to how many synthetic examples of your task DSPy will include in the prompt for in-context learning. Contrastively, `max_labeled_demos` refers to examples of your task that you provide. So DSPy can mix and match the synthetic examples it's creating by running through your program with examples that you might already have.

The extensions of `BootstrapFewShotWithOptuna` and `BootstrapFewShotRandomSearch` will try to find the optimal examples for your resulting metric. For example, say you have A,B,C labeled examples and D,E,F synthetic examples with `max_bootstrapped_demos=2` and `max_labeled_demos=2` -- perhaps A,C + E,F results in better performance than A,B + D,E and so on.

Maybe you'll also be interested in the `metric_threshold` argument to control the quality of these synthetic examples a bit further as well if you have a numeric-valued metric. :)

title: Why isn't JSONAdapter the default adapter option?
question_text:
Why isn't JSONAdapter the default adapter option?

In `dspy/predict/predict.py` the default adapter is the `ChatAdapter`:
[code]
But once that fails (`adapter/base.py`):
[code]
It switches to the `JSONAdapter`.
In my experience the ChatAdapter always fails wasting the LLM call (at least 2 calls are done for each prompt).
I know it can be set as default via `dspy.configure(lm=lm, adapter=dspy.JSONAdapter())`, but why isn't the `JSONAdapter` the default one?
author: DiyarD

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
Hey @DiyarD ! What model are you using? How complex is your signature?

For most signatures, chat adapter has a higher quality of outputs, but LMs sometimes fail to follow its structure. Hence the default strategy of using chat and fallback to json.

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
@DiyarD Yes, in our own testing, our chat adapter does have higher quality output than our JSON adapter.

There has been some discussion of the post you sent, e.g. https://x.com/dylanjcastillo/status/1867154938759155750

The tl;dr of all of these posts is clear IMO. There are three things here:

1. The prompt is the most important thing. Structured outputs cannot make up for a bad prompt.
2. The output template is the second most important thing. If the LM finds the template of its outputs confusing, the values it produces will not be good.
3. Given the best settings in (1) & (2) above, enforcing the structure at decoding time is preferrable whenever possible.

However, in practice, (3) tends to restrict (1) and (2) so much right now. I hope this changes in the future. But right now, if you want structured outputs, you tend to need (1) and (2) to overcommit to JSON specifically. Many types of outputs, like long-form RAG or code generation, are simply unusual for LLMs to see in JSON format. This does reflect itself in various anecdotes of lower quality, some of which we saw in our testing.

I hope this helps :D

comments.author: marfago
comments.body:
It seems to me that the way the ChatAdpater is structuring the output is confusing. For example in my case where I have a Signature with an output list of pydantic objects, it is adding this instruction

Respond with the corresponding output fields, starting with the field `[[ ## references ## ]]` (must be formatted as a valid Python list[Reference]), and then ending with the marker for `[[ ## completed ## ]]`.

The output is never a json string because the model follows the instruction and returns `[[ ## references ## ]]` and `[[ ## completed ## ]]`.

author: denisergashbaev

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
While we prepare a short tutorial on this: Folks looking to migrate from 2.5-style Assertions, you can now use `dspy.BestOfN` or `dspy.Refine` which replace the assertions functionality with streamlined modules instead.

```python
module = dspy.ChainOfThought(...) # or a complex multi-step dspy.Module
module = dspy.BestOfN(module, N=5, reward_fn=reward_fn, threshold=1.0)

module(...) # at most 5 retries, picking best reward, but stopping if `threshold` is reached
```

where, reward functions can return scalar values like float or bool, e.g.

```python
def reward_fn(input_kwargs, prediction):
    return len(prediction.field1) == len(prediction.field1)
```

[Feature] Optimize against multiple metrics

When trying to extract structured information from unstructured text, there might be several fields in a dspy.Signature that can be checked for correctness.
Currently it is possible to write one metric that checks for one of the fields in the signature, multiple ones or all of them during the evaluation process. However it is just one metric.
Is it possible to have multiple metrics?
Multiple metrics would give the optimization process a hint, for which fields an improval is necessary and how well a model performs for the extraction of the individual fields.
What do you think of this idea? I couldnt fin any hint of this already being implemented.
- [ ] Yes, I'd like to help implement this.
- [ ] No, I just want to request it.
_No response_
author: ratzrattillo

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
Thank you @ratzrattillo ! At the end of the day, you need a single score for optimization. Can you do an average of these metrics?

(But I think what you're saying is that, in order to optimize the average metric, it would be helpful to provide the optimizer hints about how to do a better job. That's a great idea, but it needs some thinking about this process.)

comments.author: okhat
comments.body: Yes, absolutely. I think what you're saying (and we're indeed about to do) is to allow "Metrics" to be a score + feedback. The feedback can have any type. It sounds like your feedback can be a dict of scores, but usually it's a string.

comments.author: okhat
comments.body:
Hey @ratzrattillo ! We released an experimental optimizer `dspy.SIMBA` in 2.6.15 that allows this:

```python
program = MyFancyDSPyModule()

def my_composite_metric(example, prediction, trace=None):
   score1 = metric1(example, prediction, trace)
   score2 = metric2(example, prediction, trace)
   score = (score1 + score2) / 2.0
   feedback = f"You scored {score1}/1.0 and {score2}/1.0 on metric1 and metric2, respectively"
   return dspy.Prediction(score=score, feedback=feedback)

optimized_program = dspy.SIMBA(metric=my_composite_metric).compile(program, trainset=[dspy.Example(...), ...])
```

comments.author: laitifranz
comments.body:
You are trying to call the HuggingFace API without specifying an inference point. Only some models have serverless inference API (for free, and google-t5/t5-small is not one of them) if you do not have your endpoint configured.

Since DSPy uses LiteLLM, check out the official guide to use HuggingFace models: https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers/huggingface

From LiteLLM GColab:
## Hugging Face Free Serverless Inference API
Read more about the Free Serverless Inference API here: https://huggingface.co/docs/api-inference.

In order to use litellm to call Serverless Inference API:

* Browse Serverless Inference compatible models here: https://huggingface.co/models?inference=warm&pipeline_tag=text-generation.
* Copy the model name from hugging face
* Set `model = "huggingface/<model-name>"`
* Use `HUGGINGFACE_API_KEY` instead of `HF_TOKEN`
---

An example:

```python
import dspy
import os

os.environ["HUGGINGFACE_API_KEY"] = "<your-api-key>"

lm = dspy.LM(
    model="huggingface/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", 
    max_tokens=100, 
    model_type="chat",
    num_retries=1,
    api_key=os.getenv("HUGGINGFACE_API_KEY"),
)
dspy.configure(lm=lm)

print(lm("Translate English to French: 'Hello, how are you?'"))
```

comments.author: chenmoneygithub
comments.body:
@Hangzhi Your understanding of ReAct is correct, but I think the user is asking about why `answer` doesn't appear in the conversation history although provided through the `history` field.

@nickthegroot Sorry for the late reply, but this is actually expected. ReAct is essentially a multi-stage program, with the first program only determines the tool to call, which means its output list doesn't have a field `answer`, so although `history` has `answer` field, it won't reflect on the tool calling module. However, if you look at the history of the `chainOfThought` module inside ReAct, it contains the `answer` output in the conversation history.

title: [Bug] forcing `additionalProperties` to false in JSONAdapter breaks caching for gemini
question_text:
[Bug] forcing `additionalProperties` to false in JSONAdapter breaks caching for gemini

When using JSONAdapter, the `additionalProperties: false` parameter is always added to pydantic schema of the response format parameter (either [here](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/main/dspy/adapters/json_adapter.py#L222) or [here](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/main/dspy/adapters/json_adapter.py#L233-L260)).
This is fine when calling OpenAI API, but LiteLLM removes the property in the request when sending it to gemini, see [here](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/litellm/utils.py#L2727-L2747).
Therefore the cache key is changed between `get` and `put` calls (since it recomputed) as LiteLLM.completion changes the model schema.
Couldn't the key be generated once instead of recomputed for both `get` and `put` calls [here](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/main/dspy/clients/cache.py#L220-L237)?

title: [Bug] Incomplete Streaming When LLM Omits Completion Marker
question_text:
[Bug] Incomplete Streaming When LLM Omits Completion Marker

When using `dspy.streamify()` with `StreamListener` objects, if the LLM fails to generate the expected completion marker fo (e.g., `[[ ## completed ## ]]`) for the ChatAdapter, then:
1. The last ~10 tokens of the response are never yielded to the user (lost in buffer)
2. No chunk is marked with `is_last_chunk=True`
3. The final Prediction object contains the complete response, but the streamed chunks are incomplete
The `StreamListener` class (dspy/streaming/streaming_listener.py) uses a token buffering mechanism in which, end markers are detected matching regex `r"\[\[ ## (\w+) ## \]\]"` (matches next field or `[[ ## completed ## ]]`) for `ChatAdapter`. Only when this pattern is found, it sets `stream_end = True`
Later on, (lines 188-216), the `flush()` method is ONLY called when `stream_end = True`.
The LLM might sometime not include the completion marker in its answer, in which case the research of the ending marker is never met, and thus `stream_end` remains `False`, the `flush()` method is never called, the last ~10 tokens remain in `field_end_queue` and no chunk gets `is_last_chunk=True`.
This causes the last tokens of the answer to never be streamed and be lost (or only accessible in the full prediction).
[code]
In this mocked text, the completion marker is missing. Here's what is being streamed:
[code]
it would not be too hard to have a fallback mechanism to finalize the buffer once the full answer has been generated, s.t. if no completed marker is found, we can still recover all chunks

title: [Feature] Implement ballot adapter and social choice voting methods
question_text:
[Feature] Implement ballot adapter and social choice voting methods

When using multiple agents or having multiple responses, current methods either use the modal winner (which response appears the most often) or some other multi-stage heuristic (such as [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17087)). But, there's already a field dedicated to finding the winner between multiple candidates: social choice theory. There are [many different voting systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_voting_rules) that attempt to solve various issues with aggregating preferences into a single winner, and I think DSPy is the perfect framework for implementing the ability to structure preference-seeking and preference-reconciliation behaviors in LMs.
This would be a pure addition to the package via a new adapter (and type), and new modules (presumably functions in `dspy.aggregation`, but could be somewhere else). The adapter would translate signatures into structured ballot types (either a list of candidates in order of preference, or a list of scores associated with each candidate within a given range), and then function-style modules similar to `dspy.majority` could take these preferences and find the top option according to different voting methods. An added bonus would be that these function-style modules, say using [ranked pairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranked_pairs), could also be called as `reduce_fn` in optimizers like `Ensemble`.
I've been working on this a little bit for a personal project, so I already have a fully functional `BallotAdapter` (inheriting from `JSONAdapter`), `Ballot` type, and function-style modules for voting methods like [ranked choice/instant run-off voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant-runoff_voting), [score voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Score_voting), ranked pairs (mentioned above), [Borda count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borda_count), [the Coombs method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coombs%27_method), [the Schulze method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schulze_method), and [the Kemeny-Young rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kemeny_method).
I've attached some pseudocode snippets below (truncating the full implementation for brevity).
I would love feedback as to ways this could be cleaned up or implemented better, and can open a draft PR to show my current implementation if that would be helpful, but I think this potential feature would be an exciting addition and open up some new approaches without radically altering the DSPy paradigm.
- [x] Yes, I'd like to help implement this.
- [ ] No, I just want to request it.
Adapter:
[code]
Data type:
[code]
Modules:
Within `dspy.aggregation`, we have the public functions of `ranked_pairs`, `borda_count`, `score_voting`, `approval_voting`, `instant_runoff`, `coombs_method`, `schulze_method`, and `kemeny_young`, with private helper functions such as `_extract_ballots`, `_canonicalize_ballot`, `_extract_candidates`, `_compute_pairwise_matrix`, `_normalize_scores`, `_creates_cycle`, and `_topological_sort`. There are too many to snippet here , but wanted to give the full list so far. Using these helper methods, we also could implement other systems easily in the future if desired.

We would like to get your help on adding docstrings to our public APIs. The general rule is every public API should have proper docstrings unless the API name + args is self-explainable. Currently we probably only have ~50% coverage, and we would like to move towards >90%.
To get started:
- Find a file that has missing docstrings.
- Create a github issue before working on it, so we know this file is claimed. In the created issue, mention this issue so that we can easily track it.
- Put up a PR following our [contributing guide](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) Make sure in the PR you mention your issue by adding `resolve #....` in the PR description.
- Tag any collaborator as the reviewer. If you don't know who to request review, you can tag me as the reviewer.
Some rules:
- The docstring must be 100% correct, wrong docstring is way worse than having nothing.
- The docstring follows the [Google python style guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html)
- It's recommended to include a code example to explain how to use the API/class.
- We don't enforce type hints, but we don't reject type hints either.
- Nothing in my head right now, probably more coming later...
You can refer to existing docstrings as reference, and if you feel ambiguous, feel free to tag us for questions.

```py
import dspy
from dspy.teleprompt import COPRO

try:
    my_api_key = "my_key" # use Gemini API Key

student_program = dspy.ChainOfThought("question -> answer")

trainset = [
    dspy.Example(question="What is 1+1?", answer="2").with_inputs("question"),
    dspy.Example(question="What is 2+2?", answer="4").with_inputs("question"),
    dspy.Example(question="What is 3+3?", answer="6").with_inputs("question"),
]

metric = answer_exact_match

#Initialize the COPRO Teleprompter

title: How to use DSPy with stateful agent benchmarks?
question_text:
How to use DSPy with stateful agent benchmarks?

How should we use DSPy with interactive, stateful agent benchmarks such as [AppWorld](https://github.com/stonybrooknlp/appworld) or [Terminal Bench](https://github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench)?
I'm aware that agents like `dspy.ReAct` can invoke tools. The [advanced tool use](https://dspy.ai/tutorials/tool_use/#tutorial-advanced-tool-use) tutorial shows how each task can have a different set of tools. But, these tools seem to be "retrieval-only" and does not mutate the task state in any way. Whereas in a benchmark like AppWorld, the agent can e.g. write to the filesystem, whose effects are persistent and needs to be explicilty reset should you wish to start fresh.
I'm not sure how to use such stateful task environments with DSPy optimizers. For instance, there's no clean hook into GEPA to control when environments are created or reset.
These environments are also usually process-bound, allowing only one active instance per process (thus not easily parallelizable via threads).
1. Is there a recommended or “standard” pattern for using DSPy with stateful benchmarks? Should we write a custom agent subclassing `dspy.Module`, whose `forward` function handles the task environment creation/deletion? This might work but feels like a hack. The agent technically shouldn't handle this.
2. Are there existing tutorials, examples, or design guidelines for integrating DSPy with these interactive agent benchmarks?
Any help is greatly appreciated!

When trying to use BootstrapFewShot, a ChainOfThought model, and a dataset that does not contain a context key, I ran into the following error message
[Bug] dspy.primitives.example.Example() got multiple values for keyword argument 'context' when using bootstrap
I output the context as part of the custom ChaintOfThought Module, as otherwise evaluation doesn't work. Evaluation works fine; bootstrapping does not.
Workaround is to do
input_output_dict = {**inputs, **outputs}
demo = dspy.Example(augmented=True, **input_output_dict)
on line 223 of bootstrap.py
[code]
3.1.2
author: jacco-oosterhuis

comments.author: akshatvishu
comments.body:
>  I also don't know if the context should be added, but this was my workaround

You should modify your forward method like:
```py
def forward(self, question: str, **kwargs):
    context = get_context(question)
    prediction = self.cot(question=question, context=context)
    return dspy.Prediction(context=context, **prediction)
```

the problem with your current method :
```py
prediction["context"] = context  # modifies the trace's outputs dict
```
Thus, when bootstrap tries to create demos, it sees context in both inputs and outputs which leads to the duplicate keyword error.

title: Feature Request: Add sinc-prompt format support for structured prompt decomposition
question_text:
Feature Request: Add sinc-prompt format support for structured prompt decomposition

Add native support for **sinc-prompt format**, a structured prompt decomposition method based on the Whittaker-Shannon sampling theorem. Every prompt is treated as a 6-band signal: PERSONA, CONTEXT, DATA, CONSTRAINTS, FORMAT, TASK. Omitting bands violates the Nyquist criterion and degrades output quality (empirically measured).
DSPy's core philosophy is **programming, not prompting**. sinc-prompt is exactly this: a formal, programmable structure for prompt construction with:
- **Typed fields** (the 6 bands map directly to DSPy Signature InputFields)
- **Measurable quality** (Nyquist completeness score, 0.0-1.0)
- **Optimizable** (band weights are empirically derived and can be tuned by DSPy optimizers)
- **Composable** (sinc JSON can be serialized, validated, and passed between modules)
The signal-processing foundation (Whittaker-Shannon interpolation) provides a mathematical basis for why structured prompts outperform unstructured ones: sub-Nyquist sampling causes aliasing, which manifests as hallucination.
1. **`SincSignature`** -- A Signature subclass with 6 typed input fields (persona, context, data, constraints, fmt, task) and one output field. Weights: PERSONA 7.0%, CONTEXT 6.3%, DATA 3.8%, CONSTRAINTS 42.7%, FORMAT 26.3%, TASK 2.8%.
2. **`SincModule`** -- A Module that accepts sinc JSON or individual bands, formats them, and calls the LM via Predict(SincSignature).
3. **`SincOptimizer`** -- An optimizer wrapper that adds Nyquist completeness as a metric. Wraps existing optimizers (BootstrapFewShot, MIPROv2) and validates that training examples satisfy the sampling theorem.
4. **`SincFormat`** -- Standalone utility class (no DSPy dependency) for parsing, formatting, validating, and scoring sinc JSON. Can be used independently of DSPy.
A complete, tested implementation is available: [github.com/mdalexandre/sinc-llm](https://github.com/mdalexandre/sinc-llm)
- **Structured prompt construction** without manual string formatting
- **Quality metric** (Nyquist completeness) that integrates with DSPy's optimization loop
- **Validation** that catches incomplete prompts before they reach the LM
- **Interoperability** with the sinc-prompt ecosystem (VS Code extension, npm/PyPI packages, auto-scatter engine)
- Spec: [tokencalc.pro/spec](https://tokencalc.pro/spec)
- JSON Schema: [tokencalc.pro/schema/sinc-prompt-v1.json](https://tokencalc.pro/schema/sinc-prompt-v1.json)
- Paper: [doi:10.5281/zenodo.19152668](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19152668)
- npm: `npm install sinc-prompt`
- PyPI: `pip install sinc-prompt`
